query: How can melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties be determined accurately and efficiently across the high-entropy-alloy family? State the physical rationale, expected quantitative performance, range of applicability, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive validation result that would rule out the proposed approach.

generation.hypothesis: A hybrid machine learning–CALPHAD framework, when trained on high-quality experimental melting data (e.g., DSC, in situ XRD during laser melting), can accurately and efficiently predict the melting temperature, fusion enthalpy, fusion entropy, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase heat capacities of single-phase high-entropy alloys with less than 5% error across a wide composition range.
generation.material_initial_state: High-entropy alloys prepared as homogeneous, single-phase ingots (as-cast or appropriately annealed to minimize phase segregation).
generation.intervention: Apply a hybrid ML–CALPHAD modeling approach that integrates dynamically updated experimental datasets (e.g., DSC, laser melting, and in situ diffraction measurements) to refine thermodynamic predictions.
generation.conditions: Measurements conducted near the melting point under controlled atmospheres to prevent oxidation, ensuring stable solid-to-liquid transition conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: A uniform single-phase microstructure verified by XRD and microstructural analysis to ensure that measured transition properties are intrinsic to the alloy composition.
generation.mechanism: The ML model rapidly screens vast compositional spaces while CALPHAD enforces thermodynamic consistency through free-energy minimization; together, they predict high-temperature phase transition properties by capturing both configurational effects and physical constraints.
generation.predicted_outcome: Predicted high-temperature thermodynamic properties will match experimental observations within approximately 5% error, thereby validating the approach across diverse HEA compositions.
generation.baseline: Existing DSC and laser-melting studies on HEAs that have established reproducible melting data and phase stability behavior in single-phase alloys.
generation.boundary: The approach is anticipated to be valid mainly for single-phase, homogeneous HEAs and may not extend to multi-phase systems or compositions with extreme atomic size mismatches where additional interphase interactions dominate.
generation.uncertainty: There remains uncertainty in the extrapolation to very complex or segregated HEA compositions and in predicting properties when significant kinetic effects or metastable phases are present; further experimental data is needed to refine these boundaries.

falsification_experiment.design: Systematically prepare a series of high-entropy alloy ingots with consistent single-phase microstructures covering a wide composition range. Measure their melting temperatures, fusion enthalpies, fusion entropies, volume changes during melting, and liquid-phase heat capacities using differential scanning calorimetry, high-temperature XRD, and laser melting techniques. Compare these measurements with predictions from the hybrid ML–CALPHAD model.
measurements: Fusion enthalpy and entropy via calorimetry
Volume change at melting via high-temperature XRD
Liquid-phase heat capacities using appropriate thermal analysis
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the predicted values consistently deviate from the experimental measurements by more than 5% across more than 70% of the tested compositions, then the hybrid ML–CALPHAD framework would be considered falsified for its intended predictive accuracy.

cited_evidence.text: The X-ray diffraction analyzer (XRD, D/MAX 2500 V) is employed for phase analysis of the sample prepared in this experiment. The experiment utilized Cu target Kα (λ = 0.154056 nm), with a voltage of 40 KV and a current of 40 mA. The scanning rate was set to 2°/min, the scanning angle range is between 10° and 100°. As there exists a one-to-one correspondence between each crystalline material and its diffraction pattern, this experiment combined XRD spectra with Jade 6 analysis software to determine the phase composition and crystal structure of the alloy sample. To investigate the high temperature softening resistance of the WTaVTiZr high-entropy alloy, vacuum annealing was performed on original samples and annealed samples at 900 °C, 1100 °C, and 1200 °C for 5 h and 10 h using a muffle furnace and vacuum sealing techniques. The SEM, EDS, XRD, and microhardness results of the original samples and vacuum annealing samples at different temperatures and times were compared to study the high-temperature anti-softening performance and phase structure stability of this high-entropy alloy composition.

The Gibbs free energy, G=H−TS, is the established thermodynamic criterion for phase selection, where H is enthalpy, S is entropy and T is absolute temperature. The Gibbs free energies for SS phases are described by enthalpies and entropies of mixing (Hmix and Smix), and IM phases are characterized by enthalpies and entropies of formation (Hf and Sf). The Gibbs free energies for all competing phases must be estimated, and the phase (or phases) with the lowest G gives the stable microstructure for that alloy. Smix, also called configurational entropy, is easy to modeland Hmix has been estimated for wide range of atom pairs. Sf for IM compounds is generally very small, and is often estimated to be zero. Hf of IM compounds is an essential term, but is difficult to estimate—there are no general models. Hmix is sometimes used as a proxy for Hf, but the differences between these values can be very large, and at best this approach gives only a relative ranking that cannot be used to determine G. The third-generation Gibbs energy expressions of pure Cr and V in both the liquid and A2 phases were established. By applying these expressions, the thermodynamic properties down to 0 K and thermal vacancy near the melting point can be well described. Besides, the lattice stability of Cr and V over the whole temperature range can be guaranteed. Based on the third-generation Gibbs energy expressions of pure elements, the Ta-Cr and Ta-V binary systems were thermodynamically assessed by considering the reviewed phase equilibria and thermodynamic data with the CALPHAD approach. A strategy to estimate the Gibbs energy of Laves phase was proposed by combining the theoretically computed and experimentally measured thermodynamic properties as well as semiempirical relation. Such a method was applied to C14 and C15 Laves phases in Ta-Cr and Ta-V binary systems. The calculated phase diagrams and thermodynamic properties showed nice agreement with the measured ones. Significant improvements can be observed at low temperatures compared with those from the second-generation thermodynamic descriptions, indicating the high reliability of the present thermodynamic descriptions.

decision.trend: Over the past few years, researchers have tackled core thermodynamic challenges in high-entropy alloys through (i) measuring transformation temperature and expansion behavior by thermal methods (PMC7512503), (ii) deploying data-driven and machine learning approaches to screen for desirable properties (PMC6565683), (iii) integrating CALPHAD-based high-throughput computational design for wide composition spaces (PMC8282813), and (iv) refining advanced third-generation thermodynamic models for refractory systems (PMC8950179). Despite these advances, capturing liquid-phase properties (melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting) across compositionally diverse HEAs remains difficult and computationally costly. Most existing modeling frameworks have limited validation at the high-temperature limit, and direct in situ experiments that capture liquid-phase transitions comprehensively across broad HEA families remain scarce.
decision.unsolved: Efficiently predicting both solid-to-liquid transition data (melting temperature, fusion enthalpy and entropy, and volume changes) and subsequent liquid-phase thermodynamics across varied HEA compositions is still not fully resolved. Existing databases rely on partial calibration or require extensive experiments. Balancing high accuracy with fast computational throughput for large composition spaces remains a key gap.
decision.lever: Build a hybrid ML–CALPHAD framework trained on high-quality melting data (DSC, in situ diffraction, laser melting) to predict Tm, ΔH, ΔS, ΔV, and liquid-phase heat capacities for multi-principal-element alloys across wide composition ranges. The model would dynamically refine its predictions as new experiments expand the dataset, while the integrated thermodynamics constraints from CALPHAD ensure physically consistent behavior.
decision.why: Machine learning has been shown (PMC6565683) to reduce exploratory cost by screening vast composition spaces, while third-generation CALPHAD thermodynamics (PMC8950179) can anchor the predictions in physically justified free-energy descriptions. This synergy addresses both speed and accuracy requirements. A decisive validation would be a set of systematically prepared HEA ingots with same-phase microstructures but distinct compositions, measured for melting transitions and liquid properties via advanced calorimetry; any significant and systematic mismatch between predictions and experiments would invalidate the proposed approach.
